title: Lay a full wine bottle into a wine rack cubby the gripper cannot follow it into, and push it home
instruction: Put the wine bottle that lies on the mat away in the empty space of the wine rack, neck out and pushed all the way in.
context: Stocking the bar is a listed duty of bartenders (O*NET 35-3011.00, about 0.7 million US workers) and of waiters and waitresses (35-3031.00, 2.2 million), and stockers in wine and grocery shops (53-7065.00, 2.8 million) fill the same racks. A bottle goes into a rack cubby lying down: the hand cannot go in with it, and a 1.2 kg bottle let go before its weight is inside tips back out, so the worker shifts the grip to the neck and pushes it home.
setup: Two YAM arms with parallel grippers (pads open 94 mm; a gripper is 10 cm wide), bases 61 cm apart at the near edge of the table. Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x straight out, y to the left. Wine rack: 12 mm pine boards, 34.8 wide, 12.4 tall, 26.6 deep, screwed to the table, centred on y 0 with its open front face at x 33; three cubbies in a row, each 10 x 10 cm and 26 cm deep to a 6 mm hardboard back panel; cubby floor 1.2 cm above the table, cubby centre lines at y -11.2, 0 and +11.2. Bottles: three identical full, corked 750 ml Bordeaux wine bottles, glass, 30.0 cm long, body 7.5 cm across and 19 cm long with a paper label, neck 2.9 cm across with a foil capsule, 1.2 kg each, balance point 11 cm from the base. Two are stocked in the left and right cubbies, base on the back panel, neck toward the robot, cork end 4 cm out of the front face; the middle cubby is empty. The third bottle lies on its side on a black rubber bar mat (36 x 12 cm, 5 mm thick, centred x 14, y -10, its long side turned 60 degrees clockwise from the x direction, seen from above), along the mat: base at x 21.5, y -23.0, cork end at x 6.5, y +3.0.
scoring: Checked with a ruler, a level and the trial video once everything is still. 1.0: the bottle lies in the empty cubby, base first (neck out), fully in (its cork end at most 45 mm out of the rack's front face; it is 40 mm out when the base touches the back panel), level within 3 degrees, both grippers at least 3 cm from it, and nothing has moved more than 1 mm for 1 second. 0.75: the same, but a gripper is within 3 cm of the bottle or it has not been still for 1 second. 0.5: at least 15 cm of the bottle is inside the empty cubby, level within 3 degrees, grippers at least 3 cm away. 0.25: the bottle's base is at least 2 cm inside the empty cubby (held, tilted or less than half in). 0 otherwise, and 0 for the whole trial, whatever happens afterwards, if at any time an end of the bottle came down more than 2 cm within 0.2 seconds (it was dropped, or was let go with its weight outside the cubby and tipped out; seen in the video frame by frame) or a stocked bottle was shifted more than 1 cm. Which arm does what is not scored. Full score held for 1 second ends the trial; otherwise the score at the end of the run counts.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Draw the bottle out of the cubby by its neck and lay it back on the mat on its outline (base at x 21.5, y -23.0; cork end at x 6.5, y +3.0). Check that the two stocked bottles are still pushed back against the back panel.
fidelity: Bottle, cubby and board sizes are a real 750 ml Bordeaux bottle and one row of a pine cubby rack. Each bottle is one rigid body of coaxial cylinders (body, label, stepped shoulder, neck, capsule) with its 1.2 kg spread evenly, so it balances 11 cm from the base like a full bottle; the wine does not slosh. Glass, pine and rubber share one friction value (0.6). The rack is fixed, as when screwed to a back bar. No contact-force cap is enforced.
